title: 1 Kings 22:13–28
context: Pressed to agree with the other prophets, Micaiah vows to speak only what the LORD tells him; after first echoing them, he describes Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd and a vision of the LORD’s heavenly court sending a lying spirit into the prophets’ mouths. Zedekiah strikes him, and Ahab orders him imprisoned until his safe return, which Micaiah says will not happen. Both traditions affirm that God judges justly and is not the author of sin while describing his role differently, a question already discussed at Judges 9:23 (see also 2 Chr 18).

verses.text: The messenger who went to call Micaiah spoke to him, saying, “See now, the prophets declare good to the king with one mouth. Please let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak good.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The messenger urges Micaiah, “Please let your word be like the word of one of them, and speak good.” Arminian readers note the pressure on a prophet to conform to the crowd.

The messenger may mean well, but he asks Micaiah to choose agreement over faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the temptation every messenger of God faces, to soften the word for a favorable hearing.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: faithfulness to God’s word can cost a person approval and safety.

verses.text: Micaiah said, “As the LORD lives, what the LORD says to me, that I will speak.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Micaiah answers, “As the LORD lives, what the LORD says to me, that I will speak.” Arminian readers note the prophet’s resolve to be faithful whatever the cost.

His oath sets the standard for the rest of the scene.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers echo this, seeing in Micaiah’s vow the calling of every true prophet (cf. Num 22:38; Jer 1:7).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: God’s servants speak what he gives, not what pleases.

verses.text: When he had come to the king, the king said to him, “Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth Gilead to battle, or shall we forbear?” He answered him, “Go up and prosper; and the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Asked whether to go, Micaiah first answers, “Go up and prosper; and the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.” Arminian readers usually read this as irony, since Ahab immediately suspects he is not hearing the truth.

The text does not describe Micaiah’s tone, so the irony is inferred from Ahab’s response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise usually read the reply as echoing the four hundred in a way Ahab recognizes as mocking.

Both traditions agree that the following verses show Micaiah’s true message, so his first answer is not his final word.

verses.text: The king said to him, “How many times do I have to adjure you that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the LORD’s name?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king says, “How many times do I have to adjure you that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the LORD’s name?” Arminian readers note the irony: Ahab demands the truth he has already said he hates.

He knows the difference between flattery and truth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a king who recognizes the truth but will not submit to it.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: knowing what is true and obeying it are not the same thing.

verses.text: He said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. The LORD said, ‘These have no master. Let them each return to his house in peace.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Micaiah says, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd.” Arminian readers note that the image foretells the king’s death and the army’s dispersal (cf. 22:36).

The phrase recalls Moses’ prayer for a leader (Num 27:17).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s word announcing judgment on Ahab while showing concern for the people.

Both traditions note that Jesus uses similar language of the crowds (Matt 9:36), and both read the verse as pastoral as well as a warning.

verses.text: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Didn’t I tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king says to Jehoshaphat, “Didn’t I tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?” Arminian readers note that Ahab treats the warning as personal hostility rather than a call to change course.

He hears the word, but only to confirm his prejudice.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a hardened heart that turns a warning into a grievance.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: a person can hear God’s word clearly and still refuse it.

verses.text: Micaiah said, “Therefore hear the LORD’s word. I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the army of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left.
verses.arminianNotes:
Micaiah says, “I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the army of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left.” Arminian readers note that the vision places the earthly kings’ thrones under the LORD’s rule.

The heavenly court scene is comparable to Isaiah 6:1 and Job 1:6.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see God’s sovereign rule pictured as a king in council.

Both traditions treat the vision as shared ground: what happens at Ramoth Gilead is decided under the LORD’s throne, not at the gate of Samaria.

verses.text: The LORD said, ‘Who will entice Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth Gilead?’ One said one thing, and another said another.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks, “Who will entice Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth Gilead?” Arminian readers read this as God’s judicial sentence on a king who has repeatedly refused his word, permitting and directing evil already chosen (see the Judges 9:23 discussion).

The scene is a vision, and both traditions are cautious about pressing its details.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God ordaining Ahab’s fall and governing the agents through whom it comes, while Ahab remains responsible for his choice (see the Judges 9:23 discussion; see also 2 Chr 18).

Both traditions affirm that God is just and that the judgment is deserved.

verses.text: A spirit came out and stood before the LORD, and said, ‘I will entice him.’
verses.arminianNotes:
A spirit comes before the LORD and says, “I will entice him.” Arminian readers usually stress that the evil comes from the spirit’s own willingness, which God permits as a means of judgment.

The spirit’s identity is not stated, and interpreters differ on it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that even this spirit acts only within God’s governing will and for his just purpose.

Both traditions agree the text does not make God the author of the lie, and that the identity of the spirit is left unstated.

verses.text: The LORD said to him, ‘How?’ He said, ‘I will go out and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ He said, ‘You will entice him, and will also prevail. Go out and do so.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The spirit says, “I will go out and will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets,” and the LORD says, “Go out and do so.” Arminian readers read this as God giving Ahab over to the falsehood he preferred, permitting and directing an evil already chosen.

God cannot lie (Num 23:19), and both traditions affirm this.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers read the commission as God ordaining and governing an evil agent to accomplish a just judgment (cf. Ezek 14:9; 2 Thess 2:11), without himself doing evil.

Both traditions affirm that God tempts no one (James 1:13) and that the guilt remains with those who chose deception.

verses.text: Now therefore, behold, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets; and the LORD has spoken evil concerning you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now therefore, behold, the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets.” Arminian readers note that Micaiah tells Ahab exactly what is happening, giving him a real opportunity to turn back.

The judgment is disclosed before it falls.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note that the deception is unmasked; God’s sovereign judgment does not hide the truth from Ahab.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Ahab hears the truth plainly and is responsible for rejecting it (see the Judges 9:23 discussion).

verses.text: Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek, and said, “Which way did the LORD’s Spirit go from me to speak to you?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Zedekiah strikes Micaiah on the cheek and asks, “Which way did the LORD’s Spirit go from me to speak to you?” Arminian readers note that the false prophet answers truth with violence.

His question claims the Spirit for himself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the hostility that God’s faithful messengers often face (cf. Jer 20:2).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: a claim to the Spirit is tested by its fruit and its fulfillment, not by force.

verses.text: Micaiah said, “Behold, you will see on that day when you go into an inner room to hide yourself.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Micaiah says, “Behold, you will see on that day when you go into an inner room to hide yourself.” Arminian readers note that the outcome will reveal who spoke for the LORD.

The text does not record Zedekiah’s fate.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Micaiah leaving vindication to God rather than retaliating.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the true prophet trusts the LORD to confirm his word.

verses.text: The king of Israel said, “Take Micaiah, and carry him back to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king’s son.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king orders Micaiah taken back to Amon the governor and Joash the king’s son. Arminian readers note that Ahab silences the messenger instead of heeding the message.

Power is used to suppress an unwelcome word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the pattern of prophets suffering for faithfulness (cf. Matt 5:12).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: imprisoning a messenger does not change what God has said.

verses.text: Say, ‘The king says, “Put this fellow in the prison, and feed him with bread of affliction and with water of affliction, until I come in peace.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king commands, “Put this fellow in the prison, and feed him with bread of affliction and with water of affliction, until I come in peace.” Arminian readers note Ahab’s confidence that he will return.

His words set up a public test of Micaiah’s prophecy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Ahab’s defiance as rejecting the word that warned him.

Both traditions note that Micaiah’s suffering is real, and that the narrative honors his faithfulness under it.

verses.text: Micaiah said, “If you return at all in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me.” He said, “Listen, all you people!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Micaiah says, “If you return at all in peace, the LORD has not spoken by me,” and adds, “Listen, all you people!” Arminian readers note that he stakes his credibility on the outcome, as Deuteronomy 18:22 directs.

He calls the people as witnesses.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the prophet’s confidence that the LORD’s word will be fulfilled.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: history will vindicate the true word, and the reader will see it happen in the next verses.
